item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant, will begin trading on the stock market later Thursday, a bellwether debut for a major A.I. company amid a global technology race and boom some have cautioned could become a bubble.

The company completed its initial public offering as the world’s largest stock market debut, a testament to investors’ belief in the A.I. giant’s business prowess, valuing the company at more than $1.5 trillion. Anthropic’s shares will begin trading on Thursday on Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.

Anthropic’s offering is the first time that public market investors will have the chance to invest in one of the A.I. industry’s “frontier labs,” which are developing the core models underlying the boom. The company’s offering prospectus showed a fast-growing business alongside a narrative of future growth and abundance, including curing diseases and expanding economic prosperity. Revenue soared to $33 billion in the first nine months of the year from $41 million in 2023.

The company could also pave the way for other enormous debuts, including by OpenAI, which has filed for an I.P.O. and may go public next year.

Here’s what else to know:

Initial public offering: Anthropic confirmed on Wednesday that its I.P.O. price was set at $83 a share and that it had sold more than 980 million shares, including some from its founders, for $81.3 billion. The company also planned to raise $26 billion through a private placement, bringing its total haul from the offering to $107 billion. The company’s offering topped that of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which in June raised a then record-breaking $75 billion at a higher valuation: $1.77 trillion. Read more ›

Power play: Anthropic is going public partly because its voracious demand for computing power is hugely expensive. The company has issued convertible debt to finance some of the infrastructure it needs, like chips, data centers and electricity. But this debt, which turns into equity in the future, is counted as a loss on Anthropic’s books, resulting in a net loss of $104 billion so far this year. Read more ›

Nvidia’s shadow: Anthropic’s public offering is set to the backdrop of turmoil at the chip maker Nvidia, whose chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week. Read more about Mr. Huang’s downfall, and the blockbuster earnings his company reported on Tuesday ›

Knives out: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, has for years exasperated his peers with warnings about extreme risks of A.I., even as his company has built some of the most powerful A.I. systems in the world. For some of his peers in Silicon Valley, frustration has turned to hostility. Read more ›

Corporate structure: Anthropic is set to become by far the largest publicly traded “public benefit corporation.” The unusual governing structure mandates the company balance safety and profit, creating a vast “experiment” in corporate power. Read more ›

item.title: Should You Invest in Anthropic? Here’s What to Consider.
item.description:
Buying into Anthropic doesn’t feel like your typical single-stock bet.

Unlike many initial public offering disclosure forms, this one won’t put you to sleep — but it may drive you to reach for a Xanax.

The artificial intelligence company, which on Thursday was the first A.I. lab to go public, explains the singular wager its investors are making in its prospectus, the regulatory filing that describes a new company’s business strategy, prospects and risks.

It lays out its great promise (curing diseases like cancer, developing drugs and other revolutionary innovations) and its most perilous downsides, among them “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

The notion of existential risk hasn’t prevented investors from piling into the shares of the company, valued at $1.5 trillion, which released roughly 6 percent of its shares overall to the public. Demand was far higher: The stock was priced at $83 a share, above its original target of $70 to $78, and opened trading at $111.50, a 34 percent jump.

Placing a significant portion of your wealth on a single stock is never a good idea, but there’s always the temptation to buy something when a shiny new offering comes along. Research still shows that keeping a diversified mix of stocks and bonds over the long-term is the best bet you can make.

But if you’re considering Anthropic, here are several questions to ask yourself first.

If you hold U.S. stock index funds, you’re probably already investing in A.I. — and you’re arguably even overexposed. About 35 percent of the holdings that the Morningstar Total Stock Index tracks, for example, are directly related to some type of A.I. play, according to Rodney Comegys, chief investment officer of Vanguard Capital Management and head of global equity.

That includes so-called hyperscalers, or companies like Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta that operate vast computing and data infrastructure; chip suppliers like Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices; among other categories.

Another proxy is to look at how much money your funds have allocated to the so-called Magnificent Seven, or the seven largest tech holdings, some of which have invested in Anthropic or are otherwise interconnected to the industry. This group accounts for more than a quarter of U.S. stock index funds that track the entire market, and more than a third of the S&P 500. This collection also drove 46 percent of the S&P 500’s overall return in 2025, according to J.P. Morgan Asset Management, and 55 percent in 2024, underscoring just how much they’re buoying overall performance.

Many U.S. stock index fund investors will also automatically own Anthropic stock before too long, as soon as the next week, though the initial amount will be small. Index funds try to reflect the entire stock market — so many of them will incorporate Anthropic based on the amount of shares that are publicly available.

Anthropic’s stock will initially account for an estimated 0.05 percent to 0.15 percent of the Vanguard Total Stock Market, for example, though that is likely to grow over time.

Other index funds don’t move as quickly. Funds that track the S&P 500 Index, for example, generally follow a different set of rules, which has a 12-month waiting period but also requires companies to meet profitability hurdles.

There may also be other companies that are helped (or hurt) by A.I., just as different businesses were revolutionized by the internet.

“If you look 20 years later, the companies that benefit the most from the internet worlds are something like a Home Depot or a Walmart,” Mr. Comegys added, which helped improve supply chains and sales.

Financial journalists are prohibited from investing in companies we write about. The last time I can remember buying an individual stock — Krispy Kreme! — was not long after the first tech boom. That purchase felt like an old-fashioned, Warren Buffett brand of capitalism — a company you could generally understand, and the big risk was that the chain would grow too fast.

How much can any average person truly understand about a company as complex as Anthropic, along with its founders? When you make a single bet, you’re also betting on the company’s leaders. After Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say is an asset for Chinese intelligence became public this month, its stock plummeted. Since its peak in October, the company has given up a third, or $2 trillion, of its market value.

There’s a lot we won’t know, even if our policymakers demand more transparency and regulation.

In September, an Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI said he resigned from Anthropic because he felt “neither company is acting responsibly.”

One of Anthropic’s billionaire founders recently tried to convince religious scholars that Claude could become conscious.

It’s a lot to process.

Stocks that make splashy debuts can be disappointing performers, at least for a while. Investors are essentially paying $42 for each dollar of Anthropic’s revenue. Similar companies that cost more than $40 for each dollar of revenue have underperformed the broader market in the three years after their I.P.O., even for investors who bought at the offer price, according to an analysis by Jay Ritter, an I.P.O. expert at the University of Florida. (New technology offerings overall, however, tended to outperform non-tech I.P.O.s during that same time period.)

“With Anthropic, and for that matter, SpaceX,” he said, “the valuations are reflecting very optimistic assumptions.” He added, “This time could be different, because these are companies, Anthropic in particular, with game-changing technology that’s not easy to duplicate.”

Several brokerage firms — Charles Schwab, E*Trade, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi and others — had access to a portion of the initial shares, and were offering customers the chance to acquire them at the I.P.O. price. But there were no guarantees that all customers who expressed interest would receive them.

Each firm had different rules on how they would be allocated. At Fidelity and Schwab, for example, customers needed to have at least $25,000 and $50,000 in assets, respectively, to participate.

Many financial planners have said it’s perfectly fine to take a small portion of your overall stock portfolio, say 5 percent, for play money and placing bets — as long as the rest of your savings remains diversified and thoughtfully positioned to meet specific longer-term goals, whether for retirement or college.

Having some play money can be wise — especially if it leaves you less tempted to make changes elsewhere, allowing compounding to work its magic over time.

Ron Lieber contributed reporting.

item.title: Food Delivery Is Making a Killing on Grand Theft Auto
item.description:
While Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, the protagonists of Grand Theft Auto VI, were fortifying themselves with food from fictional restaurant chains like Burger Shot and Cluckin’ Bell, real-life businesses were cashing in Thursday on the real-life players who were too intent on playing the game to cook for themselves.

“It’s all hands on deck,” said Frank Lucido, co-owner of Frankie & Joe’s Pizza in Boca Raton, Fla., hours after the game’s midnight release. “It’s going to be a really big one tonight.”

DoorDash reported that from 9 p.m. on Wednesday to 2 a.m. on Thursday, its orders in Miami — where the game is set — were up by 25 percent over a typical Wednesday night, with Philadelphia, Detroit and Atlanta also seeing double-digit increases. Its overall sales of energy drinks were up by more than 20 percent, while orders for pizza, burgers, fries and chips rose more than 10 percent.

Uber Eats said that overnight, its Miami sales were 30 percent higher than on the last two Thursdays. The company said it saw big spikes in sales of specific snacks and drinks commonly associated with gamers: orders for Red Bull Watermelon were up by 95 percent, Totino’s Pizza Rolls by 54 percent and Ghost Sour Strips by 46 percent.

At Frankie & Joe’s Pizza, before the game was released, Mr. Lucido made sure the store was fully staffed, ensured that his two best pizzaiolos would be working and doubled the amount of dough ready to slide into the oven, expecting that orders would really start picking up around 2 p.m. on Thursday.

He said he was considering keeping the restaurant open till midnight, rather than the usual 11 p.m. closing time, if the traffic warranted it. The store is also offering 20 percent discounts on delivery orders using the in-app code GTA.

“This is going to be gigantic, this game,” he said. “There’s going to be lots of young guys and middle-aged guys who are going to be staying home and playing the game.”

At the Pizza Box in Dearborn Heights, Mich., the owner, Rodney Barro, told his staff two weeks ago that everyone had to work the day of the game’s release. He also redecorated the store’s exterior to mimic the Grand Theft Auto aesthetic, and offered a release-day $6 sale on several menu items.

He expected that the store would double its usual Thursday sales. The only person he allowed to stay home was his 14-year-old gamer son. “I gave him the day off from school — he’s ‘sick,’” Mr. Barro said, laughing.

It’s not just the mom-and-pops that were anticipating bigger sales. On Wednesday, McDonald’s introduced a new service that lets players order delivery right on Discord, the communication platform most popular with gamers. Popeyes added a limited-edition Spice City sandwich inspired by Vice City, Grand Theft Auto’s version of Miami.

In the real-world Miami, Rockstar Games — the company that produced Grand Theft Auto — partnered with the local hamburger chain Skinny Louie to redecorate locations inside the Kaseya Center as Burger Shot stalls, and opened a Cluckin’ Bell chicken store inside the arena.

Uber Eats has rolled out promo codes and discounts for food, drinks and products often at the center of gaming culture — from Red Bulls delivered from 7-Eleven to HDMI cables from Best Buy and GameStop.

“We want Uber Eats to be there for fans during the biggest moment in gaming, with everything from gaming accessories and groceries to their favorite meal on launch day,” said Andrew Macdonald, the president and chief operating officer of Uber. “We even picked some of our food deals with one-handed eating in mind, so fans can keep their focus on the game.”

Similarly, DoorDash is offering partner discounts with Wendy’s and the Cheesecake Factory. “GTA 6 is more than a game launch. It’s a cultural moment that fans have been waiting years for,” Gina Igwe, vice president of brand, creative and consumer marketing at DoorDash, wrote in an email.

For gamers, especially on release days, food delivery can be vital, said Ryan Morrison, the agent of Félix Lengyel (better known as xQc), who is widely recognized as the most-watched Grand Theft Auto streamer.

“It’s a demand of their time and attention unlike anything else, and that’s why so many live and die by online delivery platforms like DoorDash or Uber Eats,” Mr. Morrison said in an email. “Felix uses it constantly to feed both him and his girlfriend during their marathon streams each day, and easily spends six figures a year doing so.”

Mr. Morrison said that for big occasions like the Grand Theft Auto VI release, Mr. Lengyel needs to stream constantly for 18 hours or longer. “A nutritionist wouldn’t be happy with most orders, as it’s a lot of fast food or things he can eat quickly rather than have to make a whole meal out of,” Mr. Morrison said.

Neil Saunders, managing director of the retail division for the consumer research analysis firm Global Data, said he expected the spike in all food deliveries to be around 20 percent, a notable rise but not to the level of the Super Bowl, which he estimated creates a 27 to 35 percent jump in demand.

“Not everyone is a gamer, and not all gamers necessarily will play the whole night,” he said. “It will probably trend into the weekend and peter out next week as most have gotten their fix of the new game. I would say it’s more like the levels you would see at college towns during the exams — that’s the parallel.”

Mr. Saunders also said grocery stores might see slower sales, except for snack foods and ready-to-eat meals.And he didn’t expect delivery apps to crash because of high volume, despite the issues plaguing so many digital platforms in recent days.

“I don’t think it’s a system-collapsing event,” he said. “You might see longer wait times and lower driver availability.”

Still, restaurants that primarily cater to walk-in customers were wary. Ilyass Berraho, the owner of Pizzeria Padrino in Columbus, Ohio, which caters mostly to a late-night crowd of Ohio State University students, said he was already seeing such a troubling slowdown in walk-in sales the night of the game’s release that he closed earlier than usual, at around 2:20 a.m.

“It was dead outside,” he said, estimating that walk-in sales were half of the usual, though delivery orders were up about 20 percent. “I know a lot of people are talking about G.T.A., and a lot of students are getting ready for it — I don’t know. Is that the G.T.A. effect?”

Ultimately, how the food-delivery business fares with the Grand Theft Auto release may come down to how indulgent gamers’ families are toward their latest obsession. That’s something Chris Hassan, a 41-year-old American travel writer living in Rio de Janeiro, is counting on.

“Haha,” he texted. “I’m hoping my wife will be sympathetic and take over meal duties for the weekend.”

item.title: JPMorgan Chase Customer Data Is Exposed in Latest Hack
item.description:
Hackers stole reams of customer data belonging to JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard, the companies said on Thursday, the latest in a string of nerve-rattling cybersecurity incidents.

The data included names, email addresses and phone numbers for some Chase customers, as well as similar information from Mastercard and Visa credit card holders. It was serious enough that JPMorgan overnight notified officials at the White House of the breach, according to two people familiar with the outreach who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.

None of the three financial institutions would specify how many customers were impacted, although Mastercard said it was a “small subset of cardholders.” The companies said the theft was the result of hackers breaching a vendor that worked for them.

JPMorgan was asked to pay a ransom to the hackers, and declined to do so, the two people said.

In a statement, a JPMorgan spokesman said “the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by vendors that was limited to some customer names, email addresses and a small amount of other public information.”

Mastercard said the incident exposed “non-payments information.” Visa blamed “a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific” and said “no payments data such as card numbers were affected.”

Cybersecurity and the technological patchwork that holds it all together have become hot topics in the wake of last week’s F.A.A. ground stop and a series of tech outages at major U.S. companies. This week, some Chase banking services were briefly disrupted, which the company blamed on a “software bug.”

Even access to nonsensitive customer information can be helpful to hackers. They can use the data to set up “phishing” operations in which scammers pretend to be representatives of trusted companies, such as banks, and trick individuals into transferring funds or disclosing personal data.

item.title: How Much Anthropic Are You About to Own?
item.description:
Another landmark I.P.O. is about to hit American investment accounts.

The artificial intelligence company Anthropic began trading Thursday after raising more money in an initial public offering than any company in history. Its initial valuation of nearly $1.5 trillion was second only to SpaceX, which Elon Musk took public in June.

You may not have personally joined the rush to purchase shares, but if you have a 401(k) or own any index funds, you will probably soon be counted as an Anthropic investor. Just how much of one?

Here’s an estimate of how much of Anthropic you may passively own via index funds:

As with SpaceX, the large majority of Anthropic shares aren’t tradable yet because they’re held by employees or early investors. The number of tradable shares, known as the “float,” is a critical part of the calculation that determines how index funds invest.

Many large tech companies, like Nvidia or Apple, will take up a more significant share of index funds, at least for now.

The largest holdings in the total U.S. stock market, with your estimated dollar exposure based on the amount you entered.

But the reason Anthropic (and SpaceX before it) will show up in some index funds only days or weeks after the I.P.O. is new rules fast-tracking the inclusion of mega I.P.O.s. (Nasdaq even includes a multiplier to increase its exposure to large I.P.O.s that start with a small float.)

The S&P 500 has not changed its rules, and will continue to wait a year after a company’s initial offering before deciding whether to include it in the index. So any funds that specifically track the S&P 500, as opposed to other broad market funds, will not include Anthropic for a while.

The calculator is based on a few assumptions that will almost certainly change in the near future. It uses the stock’s I.P.O. offer price of $83, but the stock price will most likely experience volatility over the coming days. Analysts have pegged their target price much higher, ranging from $125 to $155. So far on its first trading day, the price rose to over $110 before dropping back into the $90s.

I.P.O.s often experience a “pop,” meaning that a stock may reach extraordinary prices early on, and then tend to go down in the weeks or months after a company goes public. SpaceX, for example, began trading in June at $150 a share, soared above $200 in the days that followed, but then declined and is now trading below its initial price.

The number of tradable shares will also change over time, influencing how much of the stock is in index funds. At various stages over the next year, more shares will become tradable, usually coinciding with the company’s earnings release dates.

The total dollar valuation of Anthropic was slightly under that of SpaceX, which experienced a large post-I.P.O. price increase, followed by several days of losses. Since then, the “lockup” on hundreds of millions of SpaceX shares has expired, which will continue to increase the company’s representation in funds.

OpenAI, an Anthropic rival, has also filed to go public next year. Market nervousness has grown over A.I. investments in recent months, with fears of overvaluation and concerns over debt-fueled data center construction. That hasn’t stopped Anthropic from one of the largest public offerings in history, driven largely by tools like Claude Code, which has become increasingly popular in software engineering.

About the data

Anthropic ownership estimates use each index’s float-adjusted weighting rules, assuming Anthropic’s publicly tradable shares are worth $83 per share based on their opening price.

To estimate ownership through index funds, we calculate a weight for each company based on the company’s float-adjusted capitalization and the total capitalization of the market that an index tracks. Market caps come from Morningstar and the S&P 500’s fact sheet. The Nasdaq-100’s market capitalization was provided by Morningstar. Weights for index funds use data on Vanguard VOO, Vanguard VTSAX and Invesco QQQ provided by Morningstar. Weights for the Nasdaq-100 are estimated based on their reconstitution and rebalancing rules. Weights and market capitalization change daily.

item.title: When Downdetector Warns of an Outage, Some Hear It Crying Wolf
item.description:
When your favorite website or app stops working — and that seems to be happening a lot lately — Downdetector is often the first place to report what’s wrong.

The site, which says it tracks outages in real time for more than 36,000 companies, is coming off an unusually busy week, its maps and charts providing one heads-up after another for a global Microsoft outage, a nationwide flight stoppage, a software bug at JPMorgan Chase, computer problems at United Airlines and a disruption to Apple services.

Haym Hirsh, a computer science professor at Cornell University, called Downdetector “the thing everyone relies on if they want to know if something is not performing.”

“The scale of what they’re doing — the number of reports they’re getting — makes it believable to me,” he said. “If I’m having a question, I will go to Downdetector.”

For all its popularity and utility, the site has limits, which the company acknowledged in interviews. The charts it displays can lead to confusion and anger from executives at some of the companies it monitors.

Despite their drawbacks, the site’s alerts make their way into media reports. Its signals on the recent outages were cited by the British Broadcasting Corporation, The Associated Press, Fox News, The New York Times and other news outlets.

Downdetector started in the Netherlands in 2012, the creation of Tom Sanders, a former tech journalist, and Sander van de Graaf. It became part of Ookla in 2018, which was acquired this year by Accenture, the technology and management consulting giant.

When Downdetector launched, it would search Twitter for complaints about outages. Today its approach is broader, but Ookla is frank that Downdetector does not actually detect outages. It tracks user complaints about outages that are submitted by visitors to its website, which often pops up high in Google search results when people ask if a particular service, app or website is down.

Downdetector also tracks visits to individual company pages on its site as another indicator of a potential outage. Downdetector no longer monitors social media posts about outages, as it did when it was founded, according to Raquel Sanz, an Ookla spokeswoman.

Downdetector compares the number of user reports it fields for a particular service, such as Netflix, Verizon or Bank of America, against a base line average of the number of complaints for that company.

If the number is “significantly higher than the base line,” the company says, Downdetector displays a chart showing the spike in complaints for that company.

Downdetector does not verify with the companies that their services are actually down, a point emphasized by Luke Kehoe, a lead industry analyst at Ookla.

“We are a mirror of consumer perception and experience, and we’re holding that up,” he said in an interview. “And we do not, unfortunately, have visibility into the inner workings of individual companies, and it is just a kind of pulse of what people are feeling, and that is what is surfaced.”

That pulse can be helpful in spotting outages before companies publicly acknowledge them. And it can confirm that a problem a user is experiencing with a service is happening to other people and not the result of, say, a faulty Wi-Fi connection.

Mr. Kehoe likened Downdetector to “an early warning system” and “a red flag in the wind.”

But Mr. Kehoe added that “no single data point or data source gives a complete picture.” He counseled users — and journalists reporting off Downdetector’s charts and maps — to “definitely also refer to the official information from the company itself.”

Some corporations have complained that Downdetector’s reports can be misleading.

“Downdetector routinely shows false positives,” said Patrick Neighorn, a spokesman for Amazon Web Services.

“When one provider has a widespread service disruption, reports often increase for other services that are operating normally,” he said. “Downdetector’s home page doesn’t show how many reports each service has received, so hundreds of thousands of reports about a real disruption are hard to distinguish from a few hundred about a service where nothing is wrong.”

For example, when AT&T’s cellular network went down in February 2024, Downdetector reported thousands of user complaints about other cellular services, including Verizon and T-Mobile. But those companies said they were operating normally. At the time, T-Mobile said, “Downdetector is likely reflecting challenges our customers were having attempting to connect to users on other networks.”

Similarly, when JPMorgan Chase, the nation’s largest bank, ran into problems processing transactions on Monday, Downdetector also reported outages at other major banks, raising fears of a systemic breakdown in the banking system. But other banks said they were not having any problems, and JPMorgan Chase acknowledged that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.”

Mr. Sanders, one of the Downdetector founders, said in an interview that over the years corporate clients have been persuaded that it could help them identify issues before their own internal monitoring systems detected them.

The website, which now gets 500,000 user visits every day, makes money through a subscription service offering a variety of features for clients, including data that helps them spot trends and compare their outages with their competitors.

Dr. Hirsh at Cornell said he considers its crowdsourced data very reliable, especially for outages at large companies.

“When Downdetector tells me something is down, and it’s some sort of major service,” he said, “I tend to believe it.”

item.title: This Billionaire Just Made a Bundle Off A.I. But It Could Have Been More.
item.description:
Anthropic’s I.P.O. will mint a fortune for a cavalcade of well-known Silicon Valley angel investors, venture capitalists and early employees lucky enough to spot the A.I. start-up before it became one of the most valuable companies in the world.

Also in line to profit handsomely is Gregory Jensen, a Connecticut hedge fund executive, who has told business associates, colleagues and the occasional reporter that he saw the promise in not just Anthropic but its rival OpenAI, years ago when they were barely glints of what they would become.

Mr. Jensen, a top executive at Bridgewater Associates, one of the world’s larger hedge funds, has said that he made early investments in both companies, a result of being in the right places at the right times.

He’s told friends that his connections to some of the key players in artificial intelligence go back nearly two decades, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a private conversation. One of those links was a former Bridgewater employee, Holden Karnofsky, who now works at Anthropic and is married to Danielle Amodei, Anthropic’s co-founder.

“I was lucky enough to be the room with Dario and others,” Mr. Jensen said in a September interview with Bloomberg News, referring to the Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, “when they were talking about the scaling laws and how you could create this almost evolutionary process to create intelligence, and both the huge benefits that could create and these huge problems.”

Mr. Jensen, 52, added that he was “literally the first check to Anthropic,” an assertion that could not be independently confirmed.

Already a billionaire, Mr. Jensen told one friend, who was granted anonymity to discuss a private conversation, that he expected to make more off his Anthropic and OpenAI stakes than he had at Bridgewater. Anthropic went public on Thursday, while OpenAI is aiming its initial public offering for next year.

And yet, Mr. Jensen’s A.I. investments may not turn out to be as fruitful as they could have been.

Several years ago, Mr. Jensen told colleagues that he was selling his OpenAI stake as he was trying to seal a tricky succession plan at Bridgewater, according to three people briefed on the matter who were granted anonymity to discuss private investments. The firm’s founder, Raymond Dalio, demanded a huge payout to retire from the company, and Mr. Jensen and other top executives funded part of the buyout themselves. Mr. Dalio’s retirement was completed in 2025.

A person close to OpenAI, who was not authorized to speak publicly about the company’s investors, said Mr. Jensen no longer holds a stake in the company.

OpenAI’s most recent private fund-raising round valued the company north of $1 trillion. At the time Mr. Jensen was telling colleagues that he was selling his stake, the company was worth a small fraction of what it is now. Anthropic’s post I.P.O. valuation of about $1.5 trillion amounts to a more than 300 times return for its early investors.

A Bridgewater spokesman declined to provide a public statement, and Mr. Jensen did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesman for Mr. Dalio did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Jensen is Bridgewater’s managing chief investment officer. He runs the firm’s fast-growing A.I. fund, which includes an effort to build an A.I. investment analyst that can rival the firm’s human staff.

He has recently struck a public profile as an advocate for A.I. regulation. He co-wrote an opinion column in The New York Times in August that suggested “governments must act before the inevitable backlash fully arrives.”

item.title: Anthropic’s I.P.O. Turns Tech Researchers Into Overnight Millionaires
item.description:
When Christopher Kirchoff, a former Pentagon official, joined Anthropic for a three-month fellowship in 2024, he was surrounded in the corporate lunchroom by “bookish” young technology workers who peppered him with questions about national security, he said.

The company only had hundreds of employees at the time, and he said he was awed by what people posted in internal Slack channels about what they were working on. He remembered one employee showing colleagues an early demonstration of artificial intelligence performing basic computer tasks, including buying a Nike sweatshirt online and shipping it to Anthropic’s office without human intervention. “Everyone knew it was a door to the future,” Mr. Kirchoff said.

That relatively small circle of workers is now in line for enormous paydays.

On Thursday, Anthropic vaulted into one of the world’s most valuable companies, after its record-setting initial public offering. That has created sudden, enormous wealth for hundreds of employees who had an early hand in its assent.

The bulk of the wealth the company created during its rise will go to a relatively small group of people, who joined it in the early years when Anthropic was worth far less. Anthropic’s investor prospectus ahead of the I.P.O. not only reflected how rapidly it has grown — it had 940 employees at the end of 2024 and about 5,300 as of September — but also showed that those 940 employees stood to gain the most.

It is unclear just how wealthy many of these employees have become, but Anthropic’s prospectus provides some idea of what employees who joined just two years ago would have coming their way. An employee awarded options on $1 million of stock in 2024 would now, on average, be sitting on about $66 million of stock once it vests, according to a New York Times analysis of the prospectus. Employees who joined earlier would be worth more. But even people who started a year ago might find themselves millionaires on paper now.

The company started trading on Nasdaq on Thursday, following what was the largest I.P.O. in history that valued Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion less than six years after its founding. Its shares opened notably higher than the $83 a share level set in its I.P.O., briefly pushing the company’s value over $2 trillion.

It reached that value more quickly than other tech companies. Anthropic’s crossing of the $1 trillion mark was more than a decade faster than it took other tech titans, including Meta, Google and SpaceX.

Many of the I.P.O.’s biggest winners are the kinds of employees Anthropic has said were a priority to hire in its early days: technically savvy engineers and scientists who believed in the race to rapidly — and responsibly — develop A.I. in the near future.

Anthropic’s founders have encouraged them to donate a portion of their stakes to charity, with the company matching the shares that employees pledged. Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, said last week on the company’s investor road show that a key to its success was focusing on hiring people who were “oriented toward the public benefit” rather than “jerks.”

“We’ve been very disciplined about turning down people who are deeply technically talented but don’t fit our culture,” he said. Dr. Amodei and his six co-founders, who made an emotional split from OpenAI during the pandemic in 2020, each own Anthropic stakes now worth more than $20 billion.

Employees who joined in 2024 might have had little reason, from the outside, to imagine how big the company would become. It had generated only about $41 million in sales the previous year and hadn’t yet attracted many brand-name venture capital investors to give their seal of approval.

As Anthropic has grown, it has actively sought out employees with more typical tech backgrounds and business-focused ambitions. The company wrote in its prospectus, for instance, that it planned to hire more sales people.

Many early employees have grown increasingly alarmed about the potential havoc that advanced A.I. could cause as companies like Anthropic continue to develop it. Some signed an online petition in July urging the U.S. government to lead an effort that would “pace” A.I. development to ensure proper safeguards are in place.

Nicholas Joseph, an early employee responsible for training Anthropic’s model, pointed out in the petition that work was being done by A.I. itself, rather than by humans. “I’m not sure if or where it tops out, but a rapid acceleration in capabilities might be dangerous for society,” he wrote.

Driving those fears now is the same calculus that attracted early A.I. believers to Anthropic — that the technology was going to keep developing. Lillian Li, a tech investor at the Scottish fund manager Baillie Gifford, remembered meeting Anthropic executives for the first time in 2023. She had heard initially about the company’s potential from A.I. researcher friends, all of whom had a sense that “the next five years were going to look very different.”

“They were very earnest and sincere people that wanted to do good for the world and no one had taken seriously prior to that,” she said.

item.title: Judge Allows Trump’s $15 Billion Case Against The Times to Proceed
item.description:
A federal judge on Thursday said that President Trump’s $15 billion defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and the book publisher Penguin Random House could proceed, moving it a step closer to a potential trial.

The judge, Steven D. Merryday of the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida, denied the request from The Times and the book publisher to dismiss all of Mr. Trump’s lawsuit. He said Mr. Trump could continue to sue over seven statements that his lawyers say damaged his reputation as a successful businessman and undermined his candidacy in the 2024 presidential election.

One of the statements was published in an October 2024 article in The Times and six were from a book published by Penguin Random House.

Judge Merryday wrote that Mr. Trump had plausibly argued that the seven statements, which centered on accusations that Mr. Trump had perpetrated or benefited from crimes like tax evasion or money laundering, were “based on incomplete, minimal information.”

At the same time, Judge Merryday dismissed many other parts of Mr. Trump’s lawsuit, saying that 27 of the statements Mr. Trump had highlighted as defamatory did not reach the high bar required by a public official to prove defamation. All of the statements in a September 2024 article from The Times were thrown out, along with multiple other statements in the book and in the October 2024 article.

Mr. Trump initially sued The Times and Penguin Random House in September 2025. The named defendants include The Times reporters Susanne Craig, Russ Buettner and Peter Baker; Ms. Craig and Mr. Buettner wrote the book in the case, “Lucky Loser.” The lawsuit, which was originally dismissed as unnecessarily lengthy and digressive, was refiled in October 2025.

Lawyers for The Times and Penguin Random House had defended the accuracy of the reporting and said in their argument for the lawsuit to be dismissed that Mr. Trump had not shown that the reporters had acted with “actual malice,” a legal standard meaning they had knowingly published something false or with reckless disregard as to its truth.

“The Times is encouraged to see Judge Merryday’s dismissal of almost all claims against us,” Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesman for The Times, said in a statement. “We continue to believe the remaining claim in the filing has no legal merit. We look forward to making this argument as we continue to defend ourselves against this baseless attack on The Times and the rights of the free and independent press in this country.”

A Penguin Random House spokeswoman, Claire Von Schilling, also welcomed the dismissal of most of the case, but said the publisher was disappointed that the judge did not dismiss “several statements that have been widely reported for years and never challenged by President Trump, even in prior litigation.”

“We are confident that the evidence in this case will lead to a full dismissal and continue to stand by the book and its authors,” she said.

Mr. Trump has frequently in his second term turned to litigation as a cudgel against the news media. A $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal was dismissed in October with prejudice, meaning Mr. Trump cannot refile it, though Mr. Trump has appealed the decision. A federal judge this month allowed a separate lawsuit from Mr. Trump against the BBC to proceed.Mr. Trump previously sued The Times in 2021 over a series of articles investigating his finances. That lawsuit was dismissed.

item.title: Nvidia Asked to Sell Chips to Companies Tied to Chinese Military and Megaspeed
item.description:
Lawmakers released confidential information on Thursday showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced A.I. chips to Chinese companies for the year, as of May 11, including several firms on a list of Chinese military companies maintained by the Pentagon.

The department had received applications to sell more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese companies as of that date, lawmakers said. It approved 75,000 artificial intelligence chips for Alibaba, a Chinese A.I. giant that The New York Times reported this week has ties with a military-linked laboratory.

The release also showed that Nvidia had submitted an application in April to sell more than 40,000 of its advanced H200 chips to a company tied to Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the executive who U.S. intelligence has concluded was a Chinese asset who had an affair with the former Nvidia chief executive.

The company — New Century Lettall Data Service — is part of a network of Chinese companies with ties to Megaspeed and Ms. Huang. Its historical ownership traces back in part to an investment firm controlled by Ms. Huang’s sister, where Kang Wei, whom Ms. Huang often introduced as her husband, was also executive director.

The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for the Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese A.I. firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said. They were Nvidia’s H200 chips and the equivalent from the chip maker AMD, the MI325X.

The lawmakers, from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, took special note of the Commerce Department’s approval of sales to the companies Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies and Aivres Systems. The committee cited reporting by The New York Times that had raised questions about those firms because of their ties to sanctioned entities and noted that many of the license requests from Nvidia had listed the companies as entities that might install the systems in data centers.

Two Times reports first raised concerns about the firms in September and October, saying that Aivres was the subsidiary of a sanctioned Chinese firm that had exported billions of dollars of advanced Nvidia chips to Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Nvidia scandal.

Times reporters also visited the China offices of Maginfra and New Matrix and found them to be empty. No one present had heard of the firms, and scant information existed about them online, raising questions about whether they really existed.

The revelations that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was having an affair with Ms. Huang, along with a second woman at Nvidia, forced him to step down last week. The Justice and Commerce Departments said this week that Megaspeed was under criminal investigation for potentially smuggling chips into China.

The incident has sparked criticism from lawmakers that the Trump administration, and the Commerce Department in particular, did too little to police the flow of sensitive technology to China. Officials both in the administration and on Capitol Hill have criticized the department for maintaining close ties to Nvidia, which it is charged with regulating.

The Commerce Department has defended its processes, saying that it closely follows national security regulations. Every Nvidia and AMD application also stated that the proposed transfer posed a low risk of diversion, the committee’s release said.

John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said that the review and licensing process for the H200 spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. “Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China,” he said.

A spokeswoman for AMD said the company complied with applicable U.S. laws and regulations and had a rigorous process to ensure compliance.

The Commerce Department did not reply to a request for comment.

President Trump approved the sale of the H200 to China in December under unusual conditions. He required the chips, which are assembled in Taiwan, to be routed through the United States on their way to China, so that the government could collect a 25 percent tariff on their value and perform a security check.

Wary of the arrangement and eager to promote its own technology, the Chinese government ended up approving few purchases from its firms.

Nvidia said in its earnings this week that it would halt sales of its H200 chips to China, though it did not give a reason for the move.

In its statement, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said that withholding the information was “contrary to the national interest.” The committee plans to hold hearings next month with both Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his deputy Jeff Kessler, who has had a special role in approving license applications.

Representative Brian Mast, a Florida Republican and chairman of the committee, called Maginfra and New Matrix “fake companies,” and said that if the Commerce Department granted approvals to the firms, “obviously that is of tremendous concern to us,” he said.

Representative Gregory W. Meeks, Democrat of New York, said that the public deserved to know how decisions to sell technology to China were made, and that Congress needed to “conduct rigorous oversight.”

“Over the past month, the administration’s handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk,” he said.

item.title: Delaware Regulator Says It Was ‘Misled’ About Mark Walter’s Insurance Assets
item.description:
Delaware’s insurance regulator said Thursday that it and many other regulators were “misled” about the classification of billions of dollars in assets held by two life insurance companies controlled by Mark Walter, the billionaire investor and owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers.

The Delaware Department of Insurance also said in a lengthy statement that it was conducting its own investigation into the misclassification of assets; that inquiry comes on the heels of an investigation by federal prosecutors and federal securities regulators. In its statement the state agency rejected criticism of its oversight of the two firms, Delaware Life and Clear Spring, that has been raised by some industry analysts.

Both of the insurers, regulated in Delaware, disclosed earlier this year they were being investigated by federal authorities and had discovered that roughly $21 billion in assets they held should have been listed as investments with entities affiliated with other businesses tied to Mr. Walter and his TWG Global financial and sports empire.

The Delaware insurance department said it was misled about the true nature of these investments, and that the insurers, the auditor for the companies, and rating agencies were also misled. The statement did not comment on who had misled the regulator.

A spokesman for the insurers declined to comment. Representatives for TWG Global did not respond to a request for comment.

The statement said the department, led by Insurance Commissioner Trinidad Navarro, had previously declined to comment on the matter “due to the ongoing nature of the investigations.”

The Delaware regulator said it needed to issue a statement in response to “the recent drumbeat of inaccuracies being promulgated by individuals with little knowledge of the true facts.” The statement said, “individuals with no knowledge of the complex mechanisms by which these investments were originally misidentified” had wrongfully suggested that Delaware regulator “should have been aware of this deception.”

It is not entirely clear what prompted the insurance department to issue the statement, which was first provided to The Wall Street Journal. But it comes days after The New York Times and Bloomberg News ran articles raising questions about whether insurance regulators in Delaware and other states are keeping pace with the changing dynamics in the insurance industry, which is becoming increasingly influenced by Wall Street.

Insurance analysts and some industry executives have said Delaware regulators should have been more skeptical as to why both Delaware Life and Clear Spring regularly reported a relatively low-level of affiliated investments when many Wall Street-backed competitors were reporting high numbers.

In its statement, the regulator said: “The suggestion that regulators could predict a later scheme hidden from company executives, board members, inside and outside audit firms and rating agencies misses the truth.”

item.title: From Gig Workers to Tycoons, China Is Reaching Into Every Pocket
item.description:
A new joke has been making the rounds on the Chinese internet.

Economists have long said that China’s growth has three engines: investment, consumption and exports. The new engines, the joke goes, are raiding officials’ homes, making the rich pay back taxes and collecting social insurance payments from the poor.

The government needs money to support its rapidly aging population and for costly bets on artificial intelligence. But the economy is in a slump. The result: Chinese people, rich and poor, are feeling the squeeze as Beijing reaches deeper into their pockets to cover its bills.

Hudson Zhou, a 27-year-old freelance illustrator and graphic designer in the southwestern province of Guizhou, saw work dry up as artificial intelligence replaced human-created designs. Zhou, who uses they/them pronouns, had earned only about $4,500 for the year by the end of October — about half as much as in 2025 — but they owe more this year toward the government pension program.

Their pension bill — $1,500 — came out higher than last year because the province raised its minimum contribution for gig workers like Zhou.

China’s economy is in the doldrums, and a property bust has gutted local governments’ revenue from land sales, deepening local government debt.

Workers and employers pay into China’s pension funds, but local governments run them and share some of the cost. Strapped for cash, some have taken money from the funds. In a report released in June 2025, the National Audit Office said 13 provinces had diverted about $6 billion from pension funds to cover government wages and repay debt.

At the same time, the pension system is under strain because of an aging population. Last year only 7.9 million newborns were born in China, roughly half of the average in the 2000s and 2010s.

Beijing also has present-day reasons to encourage people to pay more into the national pension system. If people believe they will have something to rely on in retirement, they might save less and spend their money now, boosting the sluggish economy.

Xu Chenggang, an economist at Stanford, calls the government’s all-out push to collect more social insurance self-defeating. “The economy’s original problem is insufficient domestic demand,” he said. “Now the government squeezes ordinary people to plug its fiscal holes, which makes demand even weaker.”

Last year China’s Supreme People’s Court made it mandatory for employers to pay for employees’ social benefits, which include pensions, health care and unemployment. Businesses have long been required to pay into the system and automatically deduct payments from their employees’ paychecks, just as in the United States, but the law was not always enforced. The court’s decision was met with resistance from small business owners who say they can’t afford the costs and skepticism from workers who fear they will never collect.

This year the Chinese government turned its attention to gig workers, who are estimated by one research center to number some 320 million, or more than 40 percent of the country’s labor force. Only about 70 million of them were enrolled in the basic pension at the end of 2024, according to a government report.

People in the gig economy, which is called flexible employment in China, pay their own social security. The government wants them to pay 20 percent on a base income tied to the provincial average wage. That wage is often far above what gig workers earn, and it rises every year.

To get people to pay, local officials have tried cajoling and coercion. In Yichang, in central Hubei Province, the authorities threw a street festival in October with dancing robots, costumed historical figures and social security planners in matching vests. Elsewhere, the state is steering people toward taking on debt to pay for their retirement. Banks in a few provinces, working with local social security bureaus, offer loans so gig workers can keep paying into the pension fund, with the debt repaid from their future pensions. Some cities also let residents pay with Huabei, a consumer credit platform.

More ominously, the government has also pledged to mine its data to track down people who aren’t contributing. Beijing’s slogan, “leave no one uninsured,” echoes that of the Zero Covid era, “leave no one unquarantined.”

“Where exactly are these people?” Li Zhong, a vice minister of human resources and social security, asked at a news conference last month, referring to people who aren’t contributing. “We have to find them.”

The efforts have drawn widespread criticism on social media. A hashtag on why young people opt out of social insurance drew at least 48 million views on the social media platform Weibo before the topic was blocked in searches.

The Chinese government urgently needs to replenish its pension fund, which experts have said may run out by 2035. It has been raising the retirement age and contribution levels but moving slowly to fix inequalities: Retired government workers receive nearly twice the average pension of private sector retirees and more than 30 times what rural pensioners make.

For Zhou, the visual artist, payments to the pension fund and for medical insurance would amount to $206 a month, or 46 percent of their $450-a-month salary.

Zhou decided to join a growing number of Chinese who have stopped paying into the pension system, which means they won’t get money in retirement.

More concerning for Zhou now is the neighborhood committee that serves as the government’s eyes and ears at the local level.

In 2022 the neighborhood committee tagged Zhou in WeChat groups repeatedly, calling on them and other residents to enroll in medical insurance. Its workers called Zhou’s mother to urge Zhou to enroll. China Mobile, the state-owned wireless carrier, sent automated reminders.

The Chinese government has other ways to compel payment. In some of the biggest cities, residents without local registration can’t buy homes or cars or enroll their children in public schools without contribution records.

Wang, a 24-year-old trainee lawyer in Sichuan Province, has no choice to opt out. (She asked to be identified by only her family name, for fear of government retribution.)

She earns roughly $450 a month and said she had to show proof that her firm pays social insurance for her to obtain a necessary trainee certificate. The social insurance siphons off one-sixth of her pay. She’d rather not pay, she said, partly because it’s too expensive and partly because she questions whether the pension system will still exist by the time she’s old.

Some wealthy Chinese entrepreneurs say they feel like fatty meat the government takes a bite out of when it gets hungry. In recent years, even local police have preyed on businesses, sometimes with trumped-up charges, and extracted payment for debt-plagued local governments.

In July Beijing issued a new rule that demands wealthy Chinese to pay taxes on assets they hold in offshore trusts. Bill, an entrepreneur I’ve known for more than a decade, expects to owe tens of millions of dollars.

Over breakfast overlooking the Imperial Palace in central Tokyo, Bill, who asked to be identified by his English first name because he feared government repercussions, described his confusion and resignation.

He has lived in Hong Kong for more than a decade, holds a Hong Kong passport and says he has paid taxes there for years. Under the new rule, he said, none of that may matter.

He fears making the payment would amount to accepting Chinese tax residency, leaving his income and investments outside China open to taxation later.

“Being born in China has become original sin,” he said.

item.title: China’s A.I. Ambitions Are Running Into a Money Problem
item.description:
As the United States and China vie for artificial intelligence supremacy, Chinese tech companies are facing a mounting challenge: finding the money to keep up.

Like their American rivals, China’s A.I. start-ups face soaring costs to train increasingly powerful models. But while Anthropic raised more than $80 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering this week, its Chinese competitors face a far more unforgiving financial landscape.

Venture capital investment in China lags far behind that of the United States. Alibaba, Baidu and Tencent, three tech giants backing some of China’s leading A.I. companies, are grappling with negative cash flows. And investor enthusiasm for A.I. has soured. Since the end of July, China’s STAR 50 index, its version of the Nasdaq, has plunged 43 percent in a deeper sell-off than the recent downturn in American tech stocks.

China’s biggest tech companies are expected to double capital spending this year to $139 billion, even though the revenue from their A.I. labs covers less than 8 percent of that amount, according to Rhodium Group, a research firm. It forecasts that spending could top $193 billion in 2027.

“When you look at their numbers, it looks like they’re running on a treadmill that’s speeding up and getting harder to run,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, who specializes in China’s technology and industrial policies.

Much of the debate over China’s ability to compete in A.I. has focused on American export controls to restrict Chinese access to advanced semiconductors. Chinese A.I. labs have found costly workarounds, including renting data centers in Southeast Asia equipped with Nvidia chips. The Trump administration said this week it was moving forward with new rules to close that loophole.

But money might prove an equally formidable obstacle. Even if Chinese companies can find the chips they need, they must raise enough capital to buy them and finance the rising cost of developing frontier models.

Logan Wright, a partner at Rhodium Group who co-wrote a report on China’s A.I. financing, said those financial constraints “will be probably more decisive” than the chip shortage in the long term.

“The big problem is that the revenue mismatch with the Chinese models relative to capex is arguably more extreme than the U.S. case,” Mr. Wright said.

American A.I. companies spend roughly five to six times what their Chinese counterparts do, but bring in substantially more money. China’s six leading A.I. firms collectively generate about one-tenth the combined revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization.

China’s embrace of open-source A.I. has made that imbalance even harder to overcome.

By allowing developers to use and modify their models freely, Chinese companies have accelerated the global spread of their technology. But that strategy has also undermined their ability to profit from it. Companies can charge for access, only to see rivals offer the same technology at lower prices. Fierce price wars have squeezed profits further.

Z.ai, a Chinese A.I. start-up, learned that lesson in August when it released its latest open-source model, GLM-5.3 Flash. The company halved prices for two weeks to entice users to run the model on Z.ai’s servers rather than their own. But competitors quickly moved in.

By November, roughly 20 rival providers were charging less than Z.ai for access to its own technology, according to Open Router, a platform connecting users with A.I. models.

“Your own pricing power is lost during this process,” said Cheryl Wu, a researcher at GovAI, a think tank.

“No one has figured out how to make money off consumers,” said Rui Ma, a technology investor, referring to Chinese A.I. start-ups.

Another obstacle worsens China’s financing problems: access to advanced Nvidia chips, the gold standard for training the most powerful A.I. models.

From 2022 to June 2026, American companies possessed computing capacity equivalent to about 20 million Nvidia H100 chips, compared with roughly 2.6 million in China, some of it acquired through smuggling, according to EpochAI.

On Goofish, a Chinese secondhand online marketplace, sellers have advertised Nvidia’s DGX B300, an A.I. supercomputing server, for nearly $3 million — about eight times the U.S. price. Asking prices have reportedly quintupled since the start of the year, underscoring the premium Chinese companies must pay for advanced computing power.

The squeeze could worsen. Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief last week amid an investigation into a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman, was a powerful advocate of doing business with China. On Tuesday, Nvidia said it would stop shipping its chips to China, a deal that President Trump had previously permitted at Mr. Huang’s urging. The company also said it had established an export control oversight committee.

To reduce their dependence on American technology, Chinese developers are adapting their systems to run on chips made by Huawei, the Chinese telecommunications and electronics company leading the country’s chip charge.

Liang Wenfeng, chief executive of DeepSeek, the Chinese start-up that stunned Silicon Valley by developing a powerful A.I. model at a fraction of the expected cost, said Huawei’s technology is only about two years behind Nvidia’s.

But the gap remains consequential. DeepSeek would need four times as many Huawei 950 chips to match the performance of a single advanced Nvidia GB300 chip, Mr. Liang said, according to a leaked transcript of his call with investors, excerpts from which Chinese media outlets published. Huawei also lacks sufficient production capacity, he added.

“We simply can’t afford to train the largest models available right now,” he said. DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment.

Yet China’s A.I. industry has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to do more with less. Chinese researchers have pioneered techniques to train and run powerful models more efficiently. Silicon Valley has accused Chinese firms of copying leading American technologies through a process called distillation, reducing the time needed to build foundational models with expensive computing infrastructure.

For China’s A.I. companies, finding investors willing to bankroll the competition is increasingly difficult.

DeepSeek, which has raised more than $20 billion, is preparing for an initial public offering in Shanghai early next year, according to Chinese media reports. Its investors include Tencent, the battery maker CATL and state-backed investment funds.

Few competitors have access to such deep pockets.

China’s venture capital industry has been shrinking since 2021 and though it has recovered slightly in the third quarter, it is still a fraction of its American counterpart. Banks are lending to China’s tech giants, but they are more cautious with smaller A.I. labs. Credit growth has fallen to historic lows, and the central bank governor has called for slower, “higher-quality” lending.

Foreign investment has also dried up. U.S. dollar-denominated investment funds in China have plunged partly because Washington has barred American venture capital from certain advanced Chinese technologies.

In 2025, private A.I. investment in China totaled $12.4 billion, compared with $280 billion in the United States, according to the Stanford A.I. Index.

Han Lin, the China country director for the Asia Group, an advisory firm, said China had exceptional engineering talent and a government capable of mobilizing enormous resources for strategic industries.

But he added, “What frontier technology also needs is harder to mobilize — risk capital that can absorb failure.”

Even the public markets, a lifeline for cash-hungry start-ups, are becoming less welcoming. Amid the sell-off, the Chinese authorities have instructed some companies to delay or suspend planned public listings, according to Cailian Press, a Chinese business publication, suggesting Beijing is concerned about an A.I. investment bubble.

China has announced investment funds to support A.I., but much of the money has gone toward semiconductors rather than companies developing large language models.

Government investors face many of the same constraints as private ones. Wang Renxuan, an assistant finance professor at the China Europe International Business School in Shanghai, said government funds also need a credible path to returns.

Erik Walenza, a Shanghai-based managing partner at Asia Growth Partners, a consultancy advising on A.I., said it was difficult to see how Chinese A.I. companies could make their finances work “without a lot of sustained government financing.”

The challenge, he added, is not only whether Chinese engineers can build models to rival America’s but also how much of the financial burden the government is prepared to shoulder.

“It becomes more of a political will question, of how much sacrifice are we willing to make to compete in this area,” Mr. Walenza said.

item.title: Is an ‘A.I. Agent’ Coming for Our Sourdough Starter?
item.description:
Before opening his eight Upside Pizza slice shops in New York City, Noam Grossman studied with the sourdough master Anthony Falco, and has faithfully kept his original starter alive and bubbling. Naturally leavened dough, he believes, holds the secret to Upside’s signature crisp-chewy crust.

But last week, in a basement near the Port Authority Bus Terminal, Mr. Grossman grew increasingly agitated as he realized the stuff he was about to pour into a Hobart mixer could upend all that.

Leaven, a laboratory-grown product, is a shelf-stable powder that eliminates the need for the live sourdough starter that has long been the pride and preoccupation of craft bakers.

“Now that I know what it does, it feels weird to hold in my hand,” Mr. Grossman said. “This is like an A.I. agent. It feels like an existential threat to thousands of years of tradition.”

Invented by two Colorado microbiologists who are also home bakers, Leaven arrived in stores in June. But it has been quietly adopted by some of the nation’s top bakers and pizza makers over the past two years.

When added to flour and water, the microbes in Leaven begin the work of fermentation, and can carry it out it more reliably than notoriously temperamental sourdough starters. It does not shorten or replace the fermentation process — the dough still has to rise and proof as usual — but it does jump-start it.

Still, many bakers I spoke to are leery of Leaven. In professional baking, prestige is often attached to the most time-consuming, challenging and traditional methods. The mystique of live sourdough starter is the basis of the craft baking movement that took hold in the United States in the 1970s and built national brands like Panera, La Brea and Izzio.

“The emotional connection is real,” said Chad Robertson, a pioneer of the movement who founded the Tartine bakeries and just opened Altbau in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. Serious bread bakers sometimes travel with their starter, exposing it to local strains of the wild yeasts that give sourdough breads their complex flavors. After nurturing his starter in Los Angeles for a decade, he took it to Australia, Germany, Mexico and Spain, while studying and teaching. “And then to Costa Rica for a month to surf,” he said.

Although doubtful about Leaven’s ability to replicate the effect of live starter, he was curious. “If it works,” he said. “It would be the holy grail.”

Only a few Leaven users agreed to speak about the product. Others declined, including some large companies that are testing it for use in fast-food sandwiches and supermarket breads. (Some industrial bakers around the world are already using similar products.)

Scarr Pimentel, the founder of Scarr’s, the high-profile Manhattan pizzeria that first became famous for using house-milled flour and natural leavening, confirmed that he uses Leaven in all his crusts, both on the Lower East Side and in Las Vegas, with no noticeable difference.

“It’s the ultimate hack,” said Christiano Wennmann, Scarr’s head baker, who said he had kept quiet for fear that every pizza maker would start using it. “I’ve been gatekeeping it, to be honest.”

Mr. Wennmann said Leaven’s consistent results make it irresistible for a business with multiple locations and employees. “It removes a variable from a very complicated process,” he said.

Leaven is the first consumer product to encapsulate not only strains of wild yeast, but also the beneficial bacteria that live in an active starter. It’s also gluten-free, unlike a flour-based starter.

Marc Magliozzi has been fixated on improving his pizza for the 16 years Dozzino in Hoboken, N.J., has been open. He started with commercial yeast, moved to a biga (an Italian sourdough method) and then to Leaven. He said it produces a less sour flavor than live starter, but preserves the chew and umami of long-fermented dough.

“I never really wanted pizza crust to be sour,” he said, citing the tang of the tomato sauce on top. “In 10 years I think the whole sourdough pizza thing will be over.”

Still the popularity of sourdough — which generally makes tastier, more substantial and more digestible breads — marches on. Three of Time magazine’s Best New Inventions of 2026 are sourdough-related: the Sourdough Sidekick, a countertop appliance from King Arthur Flour that automatically builds a starter; Dough Dissolve, an enzyme-based cleaning product; and Leaven. It is moving into sweet baking: Sweetgreen has just released a sourdough chocolate-chip cookie nationwide.

But the term “sourdough,” like “slow-fermented” and “naturally leavened,” isn’t regulated in any way. Anything can wear the label, from supermarket white bread with a dash of commercial sour flavoring to the $60 organic rye loaf from an Austrian baker that recently made a splashy debut in New York.

During the pandemic, many home cooks fell for the siren song of sourdough. But given the work of feeding, airing and measuring a starter — not to mention the constant pressure to use it up — many (including me) found that a starter can feel like yet another domestic burden.

Just like the packets of dry yeast that most home bakers use, Leaven can be kept in the pantry and used anytime. It still took me 14 hours of proofing, stretching and folding, but the focaccia I made with it tasted better — sweeter and wheatier — than the yeast-risen version I usually bake.

Leaven’s founders, the microbiologists Cameron Martino and James Gaffney, are also avid home brewers. In an interview, Mr. Martino said that dozens of brewer’s yeasts are available, each producing a distinct style, like ales, lagers and lambics. So, they wondered, why there was only one kind of baker’s yeast on the market?

Virtually all commercial dough in the United States is made with active dry yeast, the dehydrated, domesticated version of a single yeast strain that was isolated by the Fleischmann’s company in the 1930s. That strain was selected for its quick-rising qualities: It generates the most carbon dioxide in the least time, producing a puffy loaf with a soft crumb.

But, Mr. Martino said, “you lose flavors, textures and other alternatives when you push everything into gas.”

Long fermentation with certain microbes gives sourdoughs their characteristic taste and texture. When flour and water are exposed to air and mixed with water, the bacteria and yeasts in a starter (or in a pouch of Leaven) get to work, breaking down the flour’s carbohydrates into sugars that they can eat. The bacteria are beneficial lactobacilli, the same microbes that give dry-cured meats, aged cheeses and long-fermented kimchi their umami-rich flavor.

I found it difficult to wrap my mind around how wild yeasts and living bacteria can exist in a shelf-stable product. I put this question to Scott Wiener, a New York pizza expert who teaches classes and leads tours. “If you put a rhinoceros in a zoo, it’s still a rhinoceros, right?” he said.

I pushed back, pointing out that a rhinoceros in a zoo is still noticeably alive. Is this rhinoceros, perhaps, in an artificially induced coma? “Exactly,” he said.

Back in the basement at Upside Pizza, two days after Mr. Grossman mixed the dough, it was time to bake two identical pies: one with his starter and one with Leaven.

For a first outing, the Leaven crust came out quite well — soft and stretchy, charred well on the bottom and able to hold a New York fold. Asked if he thought he could create a perfect replica of his crust with Leaven, Mr. Grossman said yes.

And if he could, would he?

“Absolutely not,” he said. The starter he uses is more than 10 years old, and has been handed off from one pizzaiolo to another, all of them successful.

“It’s not going anywhere,” he said.
